sections.0.body.0.t: Secrets scanning sweeps code, commits, pull requests and configuration files looking for credentials: API keys, access tokens, passwords, private keys and connection strings.

sections.0.body.1.t: It is the cheapest check in the pipeline and protects against one of the most common leaks: a credential committed by mistake.

sections.1.body.0.t: The first layer is pattern matching: token formats are recognizable. AWS keys start with AKIA, Stripe API tokens with sk_live_, private keys with -----BEGIN. A well-made regex catches most of them.

sections.1.body.1.t: The second layer is entropy analysis, for formats nobody documented: strings that look highly random (many distinct characters, no word pattern) near suspicious names like api_key, secret or password. It is what catches homegrown internal service keys.

sections.1.body.2.t: The third layer, when available, is active verification: the tool tests whether the credential found is valid, turning a 'potential finding' into a 'confirmed incident'.

sections.1.heading.t: How it works: patterns and entropy

sections.2.body.0.t: The classic scenario in three acts. Act one: someone pastes a production key straight into the code. It works, the test passes, life goes on.

sections.2.code.0.code.t:
const stripe = new Stripe("sk_live_EXAMPLEEXAMPLE0000000");
                              // production key in the code

sections.2.heading.t: A leak, from commit to rotation

sections.3.body.0.t: Seconds after the push, automated third-party scrapers (and GitHub's own secret scanning) are already testing the key. Deleting the commit does not fix it: the secret remains in git history, in forks and in caches. A typical local scanner report:

sections.3.code.0.code.t:
Finding:  stripe-access-token
Secret:   sk_live_EXAMPLEEXAM...
File:     src/payments.ts:1
Commit:   a1b2c3d
Entropy:  4.71

sections.3.heading.t: Act two: the bot already found it

sections.4.body.0.t: The only correct response is to revoke and rotate the credential immediately, before cleaning the repository and before discussing process. No history cleanup is fast enough to compete with a bot that tests the key every second.

sections.4.body.1.t: The structural prevention is to take secrets out of the code for good: managers like HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager or Doppler inject the credential at runtime and allow rotation without a deploy.

sections.4.heading.t: Act three: revoke first, explain later

short.t: Detects keys and passwords in the repository

tagline.t: Hunts tokens, API keys and passwords before they become an incident, including in git history.
